What are the tamper-evident packaging requirements for OTC drug products?  

The tamper-evident packaging requirements for OTC drug products are outlined in 21 CFR 211.132(b), which states that the requirements will improve the security of OTC drug packaging and help assure the safety and effectiveness of OTC drug products. An OTC drug product (except a dermatological, dentifrice, insulin, or lozenge product) for retail sale that is not packaged in a tamper-resistant package or that is not properly labeled under this section is adulterated under section 501 of the act or misbranded under section 502 of the act, or both.  

The requirements also include that the tamper-evident packaging feature described in paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be placed in a way that is unaffected if the tamper-evident feature of the package is breached or missing. Additionally, each retail package of an OTC drug product covered by this section (except ammonia inhalant in crushable glass ampules or aerosol products that depend upon the power of a liquefied or compressed gas to expel the contents from the container) must bear a statement that identifies the specific tamper-evident feature(s) used.  

The requirements apply to OTC drug products that are not packaged in a tamper-resistant package or that are not properly labeled under this section.

The master manufacturing record is required for quality control operations related to batch production records and manufacturing operations. It must include reviewing and approving all batch production-related records. If applicable, the requirement also limits the scope to ensure uniformity in finished batches of the product, as outlined in the FDA guidance. The batch production record must be maintained for at least 3 years after the distribution of the batch, as per the FDA guidance. If applicable, the requirement also limits the scope to ensure that records are readily available for authorized inspection during the retention period. The FDA guidance also states that the foreign supplier’s master manufacturing record must include calculations for relative amounts of other components based on the plant material used, ensuring uniformity in finished batches. If applicable, the requirement also limits the scope to ensure that the supplier meets requirements for verifying that the finished batches meet product specifications. The FDA guidance also states that electronic records must be originals or accurate copies of original records that are legible and stored to prevent deterioration or loss. [1][4]
